title: Sidewinder
summary: Sidewinder, also tracked as T-APT-04 and Rattlesnake, is an espionage-focused intrusion set that public reporting attributes to India with moderate confidence. Reporting describes long-running targeting of government, military and diplomatic organisations, mainly in South Asia and neighbouring regions. Documented tradecraft includes spear phishing messages carrying malicious documents, abuse of the InPage word processor format used widely in the region, and the use of shortcut files that run a script when opened. Researchers have also reported Android malware associated with the activity, as well as infrastructure built on compromised websites and free hosting. Because the activity is often low volume, evidence tends to appear as a small number of unusual document opens, outbound connections from office workstations, and new services or scheduled tasks on the host.

beginner.definition: Sidewinder is a group of attackers that spy on governments and armies. Security companies believe it works for India, but they say this with only moderate confidence. That means the evidence points that way, but it is not proven. The group is also called T-APT-04 and Rattlesnake.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group targets organisations that hold political and military secrets. It is very quiet, so a victim can stay infected for years. If you ignore a strange document or a new service on a laptop, the attacker keeps reading mail and plans. Even small teams should report odd emails, because quiet spying is hard to spot later.
howItWorks: The attacker learns about a target office and picks a document format that staff already use every day.
A spear phishing email, which is a message aimed at one person, carries that document or a link to it.
When the victim opens it, a script inside starts running and looks harmless at first.
The script contacts a website the attacker controls and downloads more tools onto the machine.
The attackers also target phones, so they can follow the same person away from the office.
They collect documents and mail slowly, and they hide their traffic on normal websites.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital night desk where the receptionist knows every regular visitor. One evening a courier brings a sealed envelope with the hospital's own letterhead. The receptionist signs for it without checking, because the paper looks correct. Inside is a form that asks for the ward list, and the courier returns each week to collect it. Sidewinder sends the sealed envelope by email, and the ward list is the information it wants.
takeaways: Attackers often use the document format that a region or industry trusts most.
Quiet espionage can last for years, so slow discovery is normal and still worth reporting.
Attribution is often held with moderate confidence, so describe behaviour as well as names.

objectives: Explain what Sidewinder is and why its attribution is held with moderate confidence.
Describe how spear phishing documents and shortcut files start an intrusion.
Explain why a region-specific document format is attractive to an espionage actor.
Describe how mobile malware extends targeting beyond office workstations.
Recognise host and network evidence such as new services and unusual outbound traffic.
Summarise why low-volume espionage activity is difficult to detect early.
